title: Democrats' advantage is clear with less than a month to go in the midterm elections
description: The U.S. Capitol stands on Sept. 23 in W
body:
The U.S. Capitol stands on Sept. 23 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump was elected in 2024, in large measure, with a mandate to bring down prices. But that hasn't happened. Instead, Trump is facing record-low approval ratings, and voters are blaming him for costs that have continued to rise since he took office this second time around.   As a result, Republicans are likely to pay the price at the ballot box next month. One month out from Election Day, the electoral landscape has shifted even more so in Democrats' direction.   They are favored to win the House, albeit with a fairly narrow majority. The Cook Political Report forecasts a five-to-15-seat net gain for Democrats at this point. That would give them in the range of 220 to 230 seats come January. (218 is needed for a majority.)   
   The Senate has shifted more dramatically over the last several months. Six seats have moved more in Democrats' direction since June in comparing Cook's ratings from then to now. When the cycle first started, the Senate was a long shot for Democrats. Now, it's within reach.   And that's largely because of the national mood, which is usually the case in midterms. Trump has just a 37% approval rating, according to an average of the polls. That's tied for the lowest pre-midterm approval in the last half century.   The only other president to be that low in that time was George W. Bush in 2006. Back then, Iraq was spiraling into civil war, and Republicans lost both the House and Senate.   Trump is also facing a historic intensity of opposition; 53% in the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll said they strongly disapprove of the job the president is doing, the highest ever recorded in the survey. That's not a great sign for Republicans with Trump insisting that the midterm elections be about him.   As it is, history is unkind to the president's party in midterm elections. They usually lose about two dozen seats in the House and four in the Senate. It's even worse for the party in power when the president's approval rating is below 50%, as Trump's is now.   
   There are multiple reasons Democratic gains might be limited, including mid-decade redistricting helping to insulate Republicans, fewer competitive-to-potentially competitive House seats, with most in districts Trump won in 2024, Republicans' campaign spending edge and the unpopularity of the Democratic Party.   That said, the headwinds the GOP is facing are very real.   Republicans have lost their edge on the economy   Economic issues continue to rate as the top problem and most important issue facing the country.   Most presidents get more blame and credit than they deserve for the economy, but the war with Iran and Trump's tariffs were choices that have directly led to increased costs on many goods and energy.   The economy is increasingly bifurcated with the wealthy doing well and regular people struggling. Wealthy Americans are seeing increases in their wealth and stock portfolios, which are dominated by AI companies.   It's a different story for many others. Inflation is outpacing wages, meaning people's paychecks aren't taking them as far. There isn't a lot of turnover in the labor market, so if someone doesn't have a job or is looking to change, it's not an easy thing to do.   Plus, many are turning against AI. In many places, it's driving up utility costs and, along with the rising national debt, is making borrowing more difficult.   All of that is coming at a time when gas prices have skyrocketed because of the Iran war, and interest rates are creeping higher. In trying to tame inflation, the Federal Reserve hiked rates this fall. That makes it more expensive to borrow money and harder to pay for things like houses and cars.   The blame for that sort of thing often gets pointed directly at the White House and the party in power, and right now, that's Trump and Republicans.   An AP/NORC poll released last week, for example, found that 65% said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump's policies than factors outside of his control.   
   Just 26% said they approved of the job he's doing on the economy.   An NBC News poll from September found that for only the second time in the Trump era, respondents said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans on the economy. (Though it was within the margin of error, the movement in the survey was clear.)   The only other time Democrats led on that question was in 2018 – the last midterm year when Trump was president. Democrats won 42 seats and control of the House then.   Add the widely negative views of the economy to the administration's immigration enforcement tactics, discretionary domestic cuts, the slashing of regulations and the government workforce, and it's all firing up Democrats.   An opposition party enthusiastic to vote is a major warning sign for the president's party, especially in a midterm year.   History is not on the side of the president's party in midterm elections   In 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, the president's party has lost House seats. On average, it's 26 seats, and it's nine more than that when a president's approval rating is below 50%.   The last three midterm elections have seen fewer lost House seats, despite unpopular presidents, in large measure because the universe of competitive districts is smaller.   The president, himself, though, has acknowledged multiple times the political headwinds his party faces in midterms.   "Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don't do well in midterms," Trump said Friday at a campaign rally in Alabama. "I don't know why. Nobody's explained it."   There are reasons, however.   First, turnout in midterms is historically about 30% lower than in presidential years. So, the voters most fired up to vote show up in outsized numbers.   Anger is a great motivator, and often the voters more aligned with the opposition party most want to register their frustration. And, as noted earlier, the intensity of opposition to Trump is at historic levels.   
   A CBS poll out Sunday found Democrats with the enthusiasm edge – 84% of Democrats and 82% of independents surveyed said they are "definitely" going to vote compared to 77% of Republicans.   What's more, a key indicator of which party does well in midterms is pointing in the Democrats' direction. Surveys, including the NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, ask a version of: "If November's election for Congress were held today, which party's candidate are you more likely to vote for in your district?"   In an average of the 2026 polls, Democrats have a nine-point advantage on this question, known as the congressional ballot test. Democrats tend to need a larger lead on the question historically than Republicans, given how districts have been drawn. But +9 is in the range of what Democrats need.   To put a finer point on it: in each of the past seven midterm elections, the party with the advantage on the congressional ballot has made gains.   
   With independents and Latinos, two swing groups, souring on Trump during this second term, that's an added problem for Republicans in competitive districts.   Their jobs are made even tougher when Trump says things like "pretend" he's on the ballot and makes the election a "referendum" on him.   The White House's theory of the case is that Trump has had success turning conservatives out when he's on the ballot, and Republican candidates need them to show up in big numbers.   But whether that's enough is going to be tested. In swing districts and some key Senate races, candidates also usually need voters in the middle to win.   The bottom line is with less than a month to go until all the votes are in, the political compass is pointed in Democrats' direction. For multiple reasons, Democrats' gains might not be as big as similar numbers might indicate in past elections, but there is no doubt that, right now, they have the wind at their backs.

title: What voters in 6 key states could tell us about the 2026 midterms
description: Voters cast their ballots inside the Arl
body:
Voters cast their ballots inside the Arlington County Courthouse in Arlington, Va., on Sept. 18, which was the first day of early voting in the state for the midterm elections.
                
                    Tom Brenner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/Getty Images
    

   
   A version of this essay first appeared in the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get the news you need to start your day — plus a little fun — every weekday and Sunday.   Four weeks from now, the midterm elections will help decide the balance of power in Congress. And ahead of Election Day, Morning Edition will be traveling to six states with some of the most competitive races to hear what voters say is shaping their decisions.   We already have some clues about where voters stand. The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll found registered voters favor Democrats for Congress over Republicans by 12 percentage points. President Trump is also very much on voters' minds, with 45% saying their vote for Congress is a vote against him, compared with about a quarter who say they are voting to support him.   
   Across the political divide, one concern keeps rising to the top: the cost of living and what it means for people's economic futures.   But this year, some of the forces driving those costs are coming from far beyond voters' own communities. The war with Iran is affecting prices at the gas pump. Tariffs imposed in Washington are reaching the checkout counter. Foreign policy, economic policy and household costs are becoming harder to separate.   
   Republicans and Democrats are both campaigning on promises to make everyday life more affordable. But voters are weighing more than their bills. Immigration and the rapid growth of massive data centers are also part of the conversation. So is the voting process itself, including new restrictions that are raising questions about how ballots will be cast, secured and counted.   
   And in several of these states, another question hangs over the races: What do voters want from their own parties, and do old political loyalties still hold? Those are some of the questions that Morning Edition will take on the road, using the six states as a window into an electorate that is changing.   Steve Inskeep is reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, two closely watched Southern states. North Carolina has an open Senate seat and newly redrawn congressional districts. Georgia has competitive races for Senate and governor after several elections in which voters have backed candidates from both parties.   
   "I am watching and listening for people who feel this election is personal," Inskeep said.   He wants to hear from people who feel directly affected by the Trump administration's changes to immigration, government, education, taxes, foreign policy and the economy.   "Trump is not on the ballot but has urged voters to act as if he is, and given the consequential acts of his administration, voters are likely to respond as if he is," Inskeep said.   
   Michel Martin is headed to Ohio and Michigan, where some of the biggest questions are about political change in the Midwest. Ohio has competitive races for governor and Senate against a backdrop of economic anxiety. In Springfield, Martin will also look at how the end of temporary protected status for Haitians is affecting a community where Haitian immigrants make up a significant share of the population — and whether disagreements over immigration are changing how voters see their own parties.   Michigan offers a different set of tests. Trump won the state narrowly in 2024, when anger over the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza was a major issue for some voters, particularly in Michigan's Arab American communities. The state also saw a sharp increase in young-voter turnout. This year, an open Senate seat and a governor's race offer another chance to see whether those shifts are carrying into the midterms — and what role younger and Black voters are playing in the Democratic coalition.   Martin calls Ohio and Michigan "two big consequential states that have always told us a lot about where the rest of the country is, and is going."   In Michigan, she will be asking what is driving voters after the state has chosen both Democrats and Republicans in key races.   "Are they mad? Sad? Or just exhausted? We hope to find out," Martin said.   
   Leila Fadel is reporting from Maine, where a Senate race could help determine control of the chamber. Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking another term against Democrat Troy Jackson. Immigration and trade are also part of the political conversation there.   "I want to know what drives voters and how much party loyalty still plays a role," Fadel said. "Are their votes up for grabs? Or are they locked in along party lines?"   Maine's long border with Canada also gives the trade war a different dimension, as tariffs and tensions over cross-border trade affect businesses and communities with close economic ties to Canada. The state has also been affected by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Fadel said she will be asking voters what they want from their candidates — and whether the party delivering that message matters.   
   A Martínez is heading to Texas, where Republicans are testing whether recent gains among Latino voters will hold. The state's U.S. Senate race has also put Texas in the national fight over control of the chamber.   Republicans redrew five congressional districts to favor the Republican Party in the midterms, including three with more Latino voters. Martínez said that this makes the party's strategy around Latino voters one of the questions he wants to examine.   "What's behind the Texas GOP's big bet on Latino voters, and will it help Republicans keep control of the U.S. Senate?"   
   Over the next four weeks, Morning Edition will report from races and electorates across the U.S., asking many of the same questions: What matters to voters now, what has changed and where is the country headed next?   Follow the reporting: Maine coverage airs today, Oct. 6. Texas is up next on Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia and then Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition and NPR.org, as well as in the NPR app and the Up First newsletter.   
   This piece was edited by Treye Green.

title: Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles raise ethics worries
description: Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegset
body:
Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced "Project Meridian: The Future of Warfare," a study of automated and AI-powered weaponry.
                
                    Carolyn Kaster/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Carolyn Kaster/Associated Press
    

   
   A new Pentagon study focusing on the future of warfare is raising ethical concerns about its authors' potential conflicts of interest.   Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced "Project Meridian: The Future of Warfare," a study of automated and AI-powered weaponry.   In addition to former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, the other two leaders of the project are SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey, the co-founder of defense technology firm Anduril. The study is expected to take 120 days.   
   "We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare," Hegseth's September 30 announcement said. "To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them."   
   The study's announcement came just days before an expected speech by President Trump at an Anduril facility in Baltimore on Tuesday.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries, at a 2023 event. President Trump will speak at an Anduril facility on Tuesday.
                
                    Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Anduril Industries builds military drones that are used on land, sea and in the air and other related defense technologies. The company received its initial funding from tech billionaire and conservative political activist Peter Thiel.   SpaceX has secured over $8 billion in U.S. defense contracts in 2026 alone, according to government contract announcements. One of its flagship products is Starshield, a military-grade, low-Earth-orbit satellite network designed to provide secure communications for the government. The company's AI chatbot, Grok, is also being used by the Pentagon.   
   There is a concern that Musk and Luckey's study would be guided by their own financial interests, said Richard Painter, a professor of corporate law at the University of Minnesota and former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.   "They all want to sell stuff," Painter said. "So if we go into it understanding that [Musk], like all the other contractors, he wants to make a lot of money selling AI to the Defense Department. Whatever he proposes, but it's not like he's doing it as a neutral public service."   
   "It's a massive conflict of interest," said a former senior Defense Department official who requested anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the Trump administration. The official said that not only do both Luckey and Musk have billions of dollars in current defense contracts, but the study could also shape the types of munitions the U.S. buys in the future. For example, it could recommend more drones or space-based assets — which both Luckey and Musk build — and fewer tanks, which they don't build.   Hegseth said he has directed Emil Michael, the Defense Department's chief technology officer, to commission Project Meridian through the MITRE Corporation, a nonprofit company that manages federally-funded research across the country. Few details were released about the scope of the project in Hegseth's one-page memo.   "MITRE is responsible for the analysis and recommendations, and will evaluate all inputs with technical rigor while applying appropriate conflict-of-interest and information safeguards," said a spokesperson for the Department of Defense. "The Project Meridian effort will examine the technologies and operational concepts required to sustain U.S. military advantage across the full spectrum of future warfighting domains across a 10-20 year time horizon."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk at a White House event about artificial intelligence on Sept. 29, 2026.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   The Department of Defense did not disclose whether Musk and Luckey have been hired as special government employees — as Musk was when he led the Department of Government Efficiency cost-cutting effort — or as contractors. The nature of their employment on the project would dictate the rules they would need to follow, Painter said.   Executive branch employees are bound by federal criminal law that bans them from taking part in government decisions that affect their own money or the financial interests of their family and business. Contractors, however, are not subject to this law.   The Department of Defense did not respond to questions about the potential conflicts of interests of hiring Musk and Luckey to lead the Project Meridian study. SpaceXAI and Anduril did not respond to requests for comment about their CEOs' potential conflicts of interest.   
   While it is common for the federal government to assemble task forces with industry leaders, the findings and recommendations of the Project Meridian study will need to be scrutinized, said a senior official at the Government Accountability Office, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press on issues they have not published reports on.   "There are safeguards that they're supposed to sign to keep them away from procurement activities and whatnot," the GAO official said. "That doesn't mean that we shouldn't be paying attention to what the project comes out with."   Additionally, the motivations for creating this task force are unclear, the official said.   "I don't know why we would need a new task force to talk about something since we've had many folks thinking about this issue for a while," the official said. "What would the point of this be?"   Another former Pentagon official who requested anonymity fearing retribution from the administration was less concerned. The official said there are always numerous efforts underway in the Pentagon and in the military services to ponder the future of war, and all those will likely feed into Project Meridian. The former official said it's one thing to be on such a panel and make recommendations, and for Congress to accept or reject them, and another for a panel member to write a requirement for a defense system and then bid on it.   The second Trump administration has employed different ethical standards than the administrations that preceded it, including holding stocks in companies that could stand to profit from contracts awarded by the government, Painter said.   "I do not know why they held on to defense stocks. In the Bush administration, we made everybody sell their defense stocks who went into the Defense Department," Painter said. "I never saw anywhere near as many financial conflicts of interest in any other administration. Even the first Trump administration wasn't as bad as this."

title: A history of presidents naming things after themselves (It's short. They rarely do)
body:
In December 2025, President Trump's name was added to the exterior of the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. Less than six months later, it was removed, following a judge's ruling that only Congress can change the name of the performing arts complex, which was established as a "living memorial" to John F. Kennedy. Above, workers stand on scaffolding outside the Kennedy Center in June.
                
                    Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump recently underscored his desire to have his name appear on the facade of the Kennedy Center with a threat. "Frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump told reporters. "It'll end up being ripped down."   Trump or his supporters have called for the president's name to appear on everything from naval battleships to airports. It's pretty rare for sitting presidents to stamp their identities on infrastructure, currency and other public assets — though history shows there are a few exceptions.   George Washington "didn't want a lot of fuss"   Discussions regarding this issue go all the way back to the first presidential administration.   
   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                George Washington is now the face on $1 bills, but that didn't happen until long after his presidency and his death. When Congress was figuring out what to put on the inaugural American coins, the House of Representatives said the president shouldn't be on the currency because that's something a monarchy would do.
                
                    Victoria Arocho/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Victoria Arocho/AP
    

   
   "They were trying to figure out what was the right balance between the prestige required to give this new office respect, but also recognizing that they were not trying to re-create a monarchy," said Lindsay Chervinsky, executive director of the George Washington Presidential Library and author of The Cabinet: George Washington and the Creation of an American Institution.   Chervinsky said the issue first came up at the federal level during Washington's presidency around the Coinage Act of 1792. Congress was figuring out what to put on the inaugural American coins, given the habit in Great Britain and other nations of plastering the reigning monarch all over theirs.   "The House of Representatives said that the president should not be on currency because of this monarchical tie," Chervinsky said.   Chervinsky said Washington shared their concerns. The president usually shied away from ostentatious self-celebration. "He didn't want a lot of fuss," she said.   But sometimes, Washington didn't seem to mind it. "They did name the federal city Washington to honor him while he was still in office," Chervinsky said.   But what about the Hoover Dam?   
   Most administrations have generally kept the names and faces of sitting presidents off public assets since then, viewing it as unseemly.   On the few occasions when a sitting president's name has appeared — such as on dams named for Teddy Roosevelt, Calvin Coolidge and Woodrow Wilson — it tended not to be the man in office pushing for it himself. "Usually it is political supporters," Chervinsky said. And the history around the naming process can be fraught.   The most prominent example of this is the Hoover Dam.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Hoover Dam on the Arizona-Nevada border was originally known as the Boulder Dam.
                
                    Keystone/Hulton Archives/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Keystone/Hulton Archives/Getty Images
    

   
   The massive public works project located near the Boulder Canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border had been known in the early stages of its development as the Boulder Dam. Hoover's secretary of the interior, Ray Lyman Wilbur, suggested rechristening the project in 1930 as the Hoover Dam, owing to the lead role Hoover had played in its planning. "Hoover negotiated the deal among the states known as the Colorado River Compact that allocated the river's water among seven states," said Kenneth Whyte, author of Hoover: An Extraordinary Life in Extraordinary Times. "So it was generally agreed that it was deserved."   
   Apparently, the president thought so too. "Hoover, I think, was pleased about it," said Whyte. "But he did not talk a lot about it at the time. He didn't want to be seen to be doing self-aggrandizing things."   But the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration was having none of it. After Roosevelt took office in 1933, his secretary of the interior, Harold Ickes, called for the dam to revert to its original moniker.   
   "Ickes based this argument on the fact that the original legislation that authorized Congress to fund the project was called the Boulder Canyon Project Act," said Marist University's David Woolner, a senior fellow and resident historian at the Roosevelt Institute, and the author of several books about the 32nd U.S. president. "And he did not like the politics of Herbert Hoover."   Woolner said Roosevelt did not object to the change. He kept his political rival's name out of his 1935 dedication speech, consistently referring to it as "Boulder Dam."   The naming coup was short-lived.   Although there was some initial opposition from Democrats, in 1947, Congress voted unanimously to change the name back. Woolner said this happened "in recognition of Hoover's early support for the project, and after the former president gained praise for his humanitarian work during and after the First and Second World Wars."   There's always the presidential library ... or "library"   Roosevelt, for his part, wasn't "particularly anxious to have things named after him," Woolner said.   But that didn't stop Roosevelt from lending his name to one major project during his presidency — the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum — "which of course he initiated," said Woolner.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The bust of President Franklin D. Roosevelt stands in front of the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum in Hyde Park, N.Y.
                
                    Craig Ruttle/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Craig Ruttle/AP
    

   
   In keeping with this tradition, President Trump told reporters at a press briefing earlier this year he is planning to build himself a presidential library in Miami.   Except it probably won't be a library. And presidential libraries are, technically speaking, public-private assets.   
   "I don't believe in building libraries or museums," Trump said. "But it's most likely going to be a hotel with a beautiful building underneath and a 747 Air Force One in the lobby."   One thing that seems certain, judging by a video rendering on the president's social media channel promoting the project: Trump's name will be prominently displayed on its facade.

title: As Trump focuses the FBI on immigration, counterintelligence is falling behind
description: FBI Director Kash Patel testifies during
body:
FBI Director Kash Patel testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in September 2026 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Win McNamee/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Getty Images
    

   
   Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.      FBI counterintelligence squads—specialized units dedicated to tracking and ferreting out foreign spies—have been hit with deep cuts across the country, even as the U.S. faces a growing array of adversaries intent on stealing the nation's secrets, according to five people familiar with the matter.   The staffing shortages are so significant that in many of the FBI's 56 field offices, counterintelligence squads only have 50% to 60% of positions filled. In multiple field offices, the number of squads doing such work has been reduced by half.   
   The cuts come as the U.S. is mired in a war with Iran, and as China—a geopolitical strategic rival—wages what American officials say is a relentless campaign to steal U.S. government secrets as well as cutting-edge research and technology. Russia also remains a formidable adversary with highly capable and aggressive intelligence services.    NPR spoke with five people familiar with the FBI's reduced focus on counterintelligence work. They all spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the topic and for fear of retribution.   
   "It's terrifying, honestly," one of the people said. "Threats are growing and we're facing it with less and less. Not a recipe for success."   The cuts to the FBI's counterintelligence squads aren't the result of a specific directive from Director Kash Patel to reduce such work or close down dedicated squads. Instead, it's a consequence of the current leadership's focus on violent crime and immigration, the people familiar with the matter say.   Bureau leaders have made clear that resources need to be dedicated to combatting violent crime, gangs and illegal immigration—top campaign issues for President Trump. Counterintelligence has dropped down the ladder of FBI priorities.   As a result, field offices have pulled agents and analysts from counterintelligence and put them on the administration's priority issues. And special agents in charge of field offices aren't backfilling those spots, but instead putting new agents or analysts on violent crime or immigration work.   
   FBI touts arrest record   In response to questions about the manpower shortages, an FBI spokesperson said: "This is false—the FBI maintains a robust counterintelligence operation across the enterprise."    The spokesperson said the bureau has expanded its counterintelligence task forces to more than 1,500 personnel, including from partner agencies and state and local law enforcement.    "Anonymous sources who criticize our counterintelligence capabilities are disconnected from reality," the spokesperson said.   The FBI also touted as successes the security at recent major events, including America's 250th anniversary celebrations and the FIFA World Cup.   In recent testimony before Congress, Patel said the FBI under his leadership has arrested more spies from Russia, China, Iran and North Korea "than any FBI in history." NPR was not able to independently verify those assertions.   While arrest numbers are one measure, experts say it isn't the most important metric of success in counterintelligence work.   
   "I want to know things like how many people were kicked out of the country because of an investigation, or how many networks were completely exposed and halted," said Emily Harding, an ex-CIA analyst and former deputy director of the Senate Intelligence Committee under Republicans.   "Sometimes the win is not the prosecution and the arrest. Sometimes the win is being able to trace a network all the way back to its source, and then being able to wrap up that network and perhaps trade them for something you want even more."   Push outside D.C.   The manpower shortages are also a ripple effect of Patel's push to get analysts out of the FBI's headquarters in Washington, D.C., and into the field—an effort that some former bureau officials say has merit.   But that effort comes with side effects. When analysts who focused on counterintelligence were moved from headquarters to field offices, many were shifted off of counterespionage work and toward work on violent crime and gangs.   
   Losing those analysts has made it harder to start new investigations, according to the people familiar with the matter. Even if agents are able to open an investigation, a lack of analysts has made it harder to make sense of the evidence and provide direction for investigators.   It is also the result of the significant exodus of experienced FBI agents and analysts from the bureau over the past 18 months.   
   Some have been fired or forced out by Patel and his leadership team. That includes five special agents and a supervisor, all of whom worked Iranian counterintelligence threats, who were dismissed days before the Trump administration launched its war on Iran.   They were among several special agents who worked on counterintelligence, including in New York, who were fired for having been involved in investigations of President Trump.   Broader drain of personnel   Those departures are part of a broader manpower drain at the bureau under this administration.   In total, the FBI has lost more than 1,500 special agents since President Trump returned to office, according to two people familiar with the matter. Overall, the bureau is down more than 650 agents from January 2025 levels.   The agents who have left have taken their experience and institutional knowledge with them—both of which are in high demand for complex, nuanced counterintelligence work, where building sources and cases can take years.   "When you lose that knowledge, you don't just replace it with a brand new agent. You lose the experience and are starting from scratch," one person said. "There's a huge learning curve for this work."   
   Counterintelligence cases are notoriously complex and difficult. Often, the goal isn't even to bring a case for prosecution, but instead to learn as much as possible about what an adversary is up to.   "Counterintelligence cases frequently go on for years and years, and they result not so much in an arrest, but maybe in somebody getting kicked out of the country or something very quiet happening," said Harding, the former CIA analyst who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.   
   It is slow, painstaking work that often involves long periods of time staring at a target.    "If you have somebody who you think is a potential Russian spy, you need 24/7 coverage of that person, and that's a lot of manpower to do 24/7 coverage," she added.   The FBI is still doing counterintelligence cases under this administration.   In May 2025, the FBI arrested a former computer specialist for the Defense Intelligence Agency for trying to provide classified information to a foreign power. He pleaded guilty this August. And last month, federal prosecutors brought charges against five suspected Russian intelligence operatives for allegedly planning attacks in Europe and the U.S., including a purported assassination plot in Washington, D.C.   But former officials say counterintelligence threats are silent by nature, which makes it hard to know when one is going undetected.   
   If the FBI misses a terrorist plot, then something is likely to explode. If the FBI misses a counterintelligence threat, the quiet theft of government secrets or cutting-edge technology just continues unimpeded.    "If the counterintelligence agents don't manage to shut down the networks, you lose everything from intellectual property to economic standings in the world, so even something as bad as real government secrets that are highly classified," Harding said.    The range of responsibilities that the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division handles is broad.   It runs the gamut from monitoring foreign spies working out of embassies and consulates to investigating what are known as non-traditional collectors—university researchers, academics, private sector workers—who are trying to steal U.S. technology and intellectual property.   It also involves investigating U.S. officials who may be selling secrets to a foreign power, such as the case against a State Department employee who was providing classified information to China.    The division is also responsible for combatting efforts by foreign governments to intimidate and, in some instances, even assassinate Americans or dissidents on U.S. soil, as well as preventing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.   
   New China cases every 12 hours   Just on the economic espionage front, the scale of the threat from the Chinese government alone is daunting.   Former FBI Director Christopher Wray said in 2022 that the bureau had more than 2,000 investigations focused on Chinese efforts to steal U.S. information or technology.   "There's just no country that presents a broader threat to our ideas, innovation, and economic security than China," Wray said in a speech dedicated to the subject.   He added that the FBI opened a new case roughly every 12 hours to counter Chinese intelligence operations.    "The harm from the Chinese government's economic espionage isn't just that its companies pull ahead based on illegally gotten technology. While they pull ahead, they push our companies and workers behind," Wray said. "That harm — company failures, job losses — has been building for a decade to the crush we feel today."   Wray, who made combatting the threat from China a priority of his tenure at the bureau, stepped down in December 2024. President Trump picked Patel to replace him.

schema.headline: As Trump focuses the FBI on immigration, counterintelligence is falling behind

title: Dems have edge in midterms, poll shows. And, Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close
description: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   In four weeks, Election Day will be here, and a series of new polls show Democrats have a decided advantage in the midterms. They are favored to win the House with a narrow majority. Democrats need 218 seats for a majority, and the Cook Political Report forecasts a net gain of five to 15 seats, which would give them between 220 and 230 seats in January. The Senate has shifted more dramatically. Six seats have moved toward the Democrats' direction since June, according to Cook's ratings. Initially seen as a long shot for Democrats, the Senate is now within reach. These projections come as President Trump's approval rating is low.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The U.S. Capitol stands on Sept. 23 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Polls are just one factor to consider for the midterms, NPR's Domenico Montanaro tells Up First. He notes that people should consider the importance of history, the national environment, political structure and money as factors as well. And people still have to vote in the elections, but even so, the momentum seems to be shifting toward Democrats, particularly in the Senate. Democratic gains in the House are uncertain, as the party's unpopularity and the fact that 25 of the 31 targeted districts are in areas Trump won in 2024 could make it hard to tip the scales in their favor, Montanaro says.➡️ If you haven't registered to vote yet, it isn't too late. Here's what you need to know about registration in your state.➡️ Find the latest election news from NPR and your local station on the NPR app.   
   A new era in Hollywood is set to arrive today as David Ellison's long-anticipated $111 billion merger with Paramount-Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery is expected to close. Despite facing months of public protests, the deal has cleared legal and regulatory challenges in the U.S. and Europe. The media conglomerate Skydance unites two film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, both more than 100 years old.   🎧 Ellison defended the merger against critics concerned about him having too much media power, NPR's Mandalit del Barco says. As part of a settlement to move the deal forward, Ellison agreed to produce 30 films a year with the combined studios, but critics remain skeptical. Concerns also linger about CNN's future, given that Ellison is an ally of Trump. To address these worries, Ellison promised to establish an independent oversight board to protect CNN from political interference. People who don't agree with the deal predict that viewers may soon see an increase in cost for streaming services and they could have fewer choices, according to del Barco.   Catherine Sweeney from NPR network station WPLN was one of seven media witnesses to observe Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in nearly 200 years. Each witness sensed that the lethal injection might not proceed smoothly. Pike's attorneys had requested the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow hanging instead due to concerns that her platelet disorder and small veins would make the injection painful and ineffective. Sweeney describes what she saw and heard throughout that day.   
   Russian authorities are urging people to remain calm after a worker at an infectious diseases institute in Siberia died from a mysterious illness, raising speculation about a potential plague outbreak. Last Tuesday, a 28-year-old female lab worker at the anti-plague Research Institute in Irkutsk fell ill and died two days later. Questions remain over the cause of her death. Here's what we do and don't know.   On the road to the midterms   by Majd Al-Waheidi, Morning Edition and Up First digital editor   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        NPR
    

   
   Four weeks from now, the midterm election will help decide the balance of power in Congress. And ahead of Election Day, Morning Edition will be traveling to six states with some of the most competitive races to hear what voters say is shaping their decisions.   Steve Inskeep is reporting from North Carolina and Georgia. Michel Martin is headed to Ohio and Michigan. Leila Fadel is reporting from Maine. And A Martínez is heading to Texas.   Across the political divide, one concern keeps rising to the top: the cost of living and what it means for people's economic futures.   But voters are weighing more than their bills. Immigration and the rapid growth of massive data centers are also part of the conversation. So is the voting process itself, including new restrictions that are raising questions about how ballots will be cast, secured and counted.   Over the next four weeks, Morning Edition will report from different races and electorates across the country, asking many of the same questions: What matters to voters now, what has changed and where is the country headed next?   So what will our hosts be listening for when Morning Edition hits the road? We asked them. Here are four things on their minds:   Steve Inskeep: "I am watching and listening for people who feel this election is personal. By which I mean that, beyond their general opinion of the state of the country, they feel they were directly affected by the events of the past two years — the Trump administration's dramatic moves to reshape immigration, government, education, science, research, the military, emergency management, taxes, foreign policy and the economy at large.   
   Michel Martin: "Ohio is also a key location for the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign, as well as a leading industrial and logistics hub, a place where we should be able to see how the administration's economic policies are playing out. Trump isn't on the ballot, but his policies are. So let's see how that's going.   "Michigan was once considered a big part of the Democrats' 'Blue Wall,' but in recent years has chosen both Democrats and Republicans in key races. And the Democratic base has had beef with the national party. So what's driving voters? Are they mad? Sad? Or just exhausted? We hope to find out."   Leila Fadel: "The path to controlling the Senate in part runs through Maine, and that's why we're reporting in the state before the midterm elections. I want to know what drives voters, and how much party loyalty still plays a role. Are their votes up for grabs? Or are they locked in along party lines?"   "This is a state that's seen some of the worst of the immigration crackdown; a man was killed by ICE. It has one of the longest borders with Canada, and so the trade war hits differently. The Democratic candidate Troy Jackson is facing incumbent Susan Collins, who has won her state five times before. So, we'll be asking what people want from their candidate and if it matters which party that resonating message comes from."   A Martínez: "Texas Republicans gerrymandered five congressional districts to favor the GOP in the upcoming midterms. In three of them, the new maps created more Latino voters."   "What's behind the Texas GOP's big bet on Latino voters, and will it help Republicans keep control of the U.S. Senate?"   Follow the reporting: Maine coverage airs today. Texas is up next on Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, and Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in the Up First newsletter.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Bavarian breakfast that's meat and carb heavy — and not for the faint of heart.
                
                    Esme Nicholson/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Esme Nicholson/NPR
    

   
   A new NPR series is taking readers and listeners to breakfast tables around the world. In Munich, Germany, a Bavarian breakfast typically consists of boiled veal sausage, sweet mustard and a giant pretzel, all washed down with beer. Demetrios Kyriakides, who spent a year researching Bavarian breakfast joints in Munich, says the ambiance of Gemütlichkeit, which describes conviviality, is just as important as the food. A meal is often accompanied by brass oom-pah-pah music. This feast is usually finished before the church bells ring at midday, signaling that all good things must come to an end. Check out these photos of breakfast in Munich.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dance Theatre of Harlem dancer stars in the titular role for the company's revival of its 1982 Firebird production, wearing a costume designed by the late Geoffrey Holder.
                
                    Nir Arieli/Dance Theatre of Harlem
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nir Arieli/Dance Theatre of Harlem
    

   
   Under artistic director Robert Garland, Dance Theatre of Harlem is embarking on a new era by reviving its landmark 1982 production of Firebird for an international tour.Biologists at the University of Massachusetts Amherst have found what may potentially be the world's loudest birds, and they all live in Brazil. (via WBUR)Scientist Olivia Sanderfoot wants to establish a new field called "smoke ecology," which studies the effects of wildfire smoke on wildlife and seeks ways to mitigate its impacts.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case
description: Louie Delaware walks through an open are
body:
Louie Delaware walks through an open area near his rebuilt home in Louisville, Colo. The landscape includes areas where homes destroyed in the Marshall Fire have not been rebuilt. The costs of adapting to climate-related impacts are part of Boulder County's claims against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy.
                
                    Jimena Peck for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jimena Peck for NPR
    

   
   A new Supreme Court term began Monday with arguments in a blockbuster case about the reach of state power.   Boulder, Colo., is suing two big energy companies, arguing they deceived people about the harms of fossil fuels and contributed to disasters that cost Boulder a lot of time and money.   The dispute could have ramifications far beyond the climate, to other areas where states are trying to hold companies accountable for their alleged harms to local communities.   In 2018, Boulder County slapped the giant energy companies Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil with a lawsuit. Boulder argued the companies and a trade group knew decades ago that fossil fuels would hurt the environment, raising the risk of floods, extreme heat and wildfires.   
   Three years later, in late December 2021, the Marshall Fire swept across the county.   
   Daryl McCool left her home southeast of Boulder so fast she couldn't remember whether she locked the front door.   As it turned out, that didn't matter.   "There's basically nothing left," McCool said. "A 2,000-degree fire burns everything, like coins were melted, bicycles melted."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Daryl McCool poses inside her rebuilt home in Superior, Colorado. Her previous home was destroyed in the Marshall Fire, which swept through Superior and Louisville on Dec. 30, 2021.
                
                    Jimena Peck for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jimena Peck for NPR
    

   
   The historic 1901 house where she raised her son had turned to ash. McCool spent years helping her neighbors file insurance papers and apply for grants to rebuild their homes. Now, she tries to educate people about the human costs of climate change.   
   Who has power to grapple with climate change   Corey Riday-White is legal director at the Center for Climate Integrity. It supports communities trying to hold oil companies responsible for environmental harms.   "This case represents whether or not we believe as a society that corporations should be held to the same standards that all of us are, right?" Riday-White said. "If you know you are going to cause harm, and you don't tell someone, then you should help clean up that harm."   Boulder's lawsuit has not gone to trial; it's still in the early stages in the Colorado court system. But the energy companies are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the case now. The companies say only the federal government has the power and expertise to grapple with something as big as climate change. To let Boulder's case proceed, they say, would have huge implications.   
   Todd Zywicki is a professor at the Antonin Scalia Law School at George Mason University.   "This is about whether a bunch of rich hippies in Boulder County are allowed to dictate environment and energy policy to the entire rest of the world," Zywicki said in a recent webinar about the case.   Exxon referred NPR to the company's court filings. Suncor didn't respond to an email requesting comment.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Daryl McCool points to photographs displayed in her rebuilt home in Superior, Colorado. McCool lost the small, single-story historic miner's shack where she and her family had lived for 25 years when it was destroyed in the Marshall Fire on Dec. 30, 2021. The fire is part of the broader climate-related costs facing Colorado communities.
                
                    Jimena Peck for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jimena Peck for NPR
    

   
   The Trump administration is siding with the energy companies, arguing global warming is a global issue.   "Essentially Boulder claims that Colorado can reach around the United States, the entirety of the United States, and to my mind, regulate production everywhere by attaching liability to it," said Sai Prakash, a law professor at the University of Virginia who filed a friend of the court brief backing Suncor and Exxon.   "If Boulder can attach liability to these two companies … I think it can attach liability to thousands of others as well," Prakash said.   
   Seeking to recover past and future costs   Boulder argues it's not suing to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Rather, it says, it wants to recover past and future costs of repairs, emergency services, and property damage.   Dozens of similar cases where states and municipalities are suing energy giants have been moving through the courts at early stages. Any Supreme Court ruling could have repercussions for many of them.   Jonathan Adler, a law professor at the College of William and Mary, points out in court papers that Congress has the authority to override state laws here, but federal lawmakers haven't done anything.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A newly rebuilt home stands next to an empty lot in the Louisville neighborhood. Wildfires are among the climate-related impacts Boulder County cites in its lawsuit against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy.
                
                    Jimena Peck for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jimena Peck for NPR
    

   
   Corey Riday-White, of the Center for Climate Integrity, said for the justices interested in ruling based on the text of the Constitution or federal statutes, there is not much to support Suncor and Exxon.   "They want the court to say, you can't bring any of these cases in court because this is the purview of the federal government," Riday-White said. "The problem is the big oil companies can't point to any legal doctrine, any statute, any part of the Constitution that backs up that finding."   
   How the court decides to draw the lines on state power could influence a lot more than climate litigation, according to Deepak Gupta, who regularly argues before the high court.   "Pollution by forever chemicals, nuisance suits over AI data centers, opioids litigation, all of these are about the local effects of conduct that runs across borders," Gupta said at a recent briefing sponsored by Georgetown's Supreme Court Institute.   The conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court may be uncomfortable letting state juries decide some of these pressing issues. But legal experts say they're not sure quite how the justices might shape a decision in the Boulder case.   Louie Delaware, who lost his Boulder-area home in the Marshall fire, said he plans to be at the Supreme Court Monday as it hears arguments in the case. Delaware said he tried to fight off the fire with a garden hose, but he lacked the appropriate protective gear, so he realized that he needed to drive away quickly.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Louie Delaware stands in his rebuilt home in Louisville, Colorado, more than four years after the Marshall Fire destroyed the family's previous house. Boulder County says Colorado communities are facing rising costs from wildfires, drought, extreme heat and other climate impacts.
                
                    Jimena Peck for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jimena Peck for NPR
    

   
   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Louie Delaware holds his phone showing a photo of his family outside of their burned home after the Marshall Fire, which destroyed more than 1,100 homes in Louisville, Superior and unincorporated Boulder County.
                
                    Jimena Peck for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jimena Peck for NPR
    

   
   "You know it's our responsibility to leave things better for the next generation," Delaware said. "And the way we're going right now is counter to what that's been in the past."   Last-minute Alito recusal   In a surprise move, the court notified lawyers in the case just one week before argument that Justice Samuel Alito had decided not to participate. The court clerk provided no explanation in his letter. But environmental organizations and watchdog groups had been calling for Alito's recusal because of his investments in Phillips 66 and ConocoPhillips.   Justin Kloczko of the group Consumer Watchdog said the decision is "the right decision, and one he should have made from the start."   
   "The public should not have to wonder whether a justice's personal investments could benefit from a ruling that shields the fossil-fuel industry from liability," Kloczko said in a written statement.   Alito's decision to step aside means eight justices will hear the case. In the matter of a 4-4 tie, that means the decision of the Colorado Supreme Court—allowing Boulder's lawsuit to proceed—will prevail.   But the high court may have left itself another option: among the questions the justices said they'll consider is whether they have jurisdiction to hear the Suncor case now, because it's still at an early stage in Colorado state courts.

schema.headline: Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case

title: Disney, ABC battle Trump's FCC in court over free speech protections
description: A demonstrator waves a "Protect Free Spe
body:
A demonstrator waves a "Protect Free Speech" sign following a protest against the suspension of the "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" show, held near the theater where the show is produced in Hollywood, on September 22, 2025 in Los Angeles, California.
                
                    Mario Tama/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mario Tama/Getty Images North America
    

   
   A federal court in Washington, D.C., is to play host to a legal battle Tuesday morning pitting the Walt Disney Co. against the nation's chief broadcast regulator over just how far First Amendment protections can go during the presidency of Donald Trump.   
   President Trump has repeatedly called for Disney's ABC TV to fire late night comedian Jimmy Kimmel, who has consistently mocked the president. Trump has also routinely denounced ABC's The View, accusing it of being liberal and unfair.   Trump had earlier sued the network, before returning to office, over incorrect statements anchor George Stephanopoulos made about the verdicts in writer E. Jean Carroll's two lawsuits against Trump. ABC paid $16 million in a December 2024 settlement, including legal fees, to resolve that a month before Trump went back to the White House. But new Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro has authorized a high-stakes fight against the administration in court.   
   Brendan Carr, whom Trump elevated to be the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, has echoed the president's complaints. And under Carr, the FCC is moving to review Disney's ownership of all eight of the stations it owns, as part of the ABC Network, years ahead of schedule. That followed months of social media posts from Trump urging that the FCC strip ABC of its station licenses.   "There's not even a question as to what Carr is doing. What Carr is doing is unconstitutional," says Mark Fowler, a Republican former FCC chair under President Ronald Reagan. Fowler has filed a statement to aid ABC's lawsuit in which he likened Carr's actions to censorship. "The First Amendment is very plain in its wording and its meaning," he says.   
   Technically, networks do not require licenses from the federal government to operate. Stations do need them to utilize publicly owned airwaves. They are perennially reviewed on a staggered basis and are typically renewed without much fanfare.   Carr has cited the requirement of stations to serve the "public interest," initiated investigations of Disney's diversity, equity and inclusion policies, and, though he says the license review is not linked to ABC's content, he has blasted the network as biased.   Disney and ABC are seeking to get U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan to issue an order preventing the FCC from accelerating the typical review process. She had compelled the FCC to hold off from moving ahead until this hearing. Media advocates, FCC veterans and legal observers say the move to challenge all ABC's local licenses at once is unprecedented. And were it to be successful, it would hurt ABC badly in the bottom line. Six of those eight stations are in major media markets and contribute significantly to the network's bottom line.   
   "The overreaching by the FCC is one of the greatest threats right now that's facing journalism," says Bruce Brown, the president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.   In an interview with NPR in August, Carr said that the agency has not decided whether to pull the station licenses from ABC. Instead, he said, ABC is complaining about his drive to take the "public interest" component of the law seriously. And he said that the network is getting ahead of itself. The agency has not yet taken any action against ABC's licenses — merely sped up their review.   
   That question may consume part of the legal wrangling on Tuesday as it will help determine whether ABC and Disney have standing to sue.   Conservative groups, including the fundraising outfits for U.S. Senate and House Republican candidates, filed briefs to support the FCC, and by extension, the president's complaints about bias.   "By any commonsense standard, evidence of broadcaster intent to advance the candidacies of Democratic Party figures on The View is not merely present, but overwhelming," the Republican fundraising committees say in a court filing.   Even so, several groups often affiliated with conservatives have weighed in against the Justice Department's case, including the Cato Institute, the Competitive Enterprise Institute and the Institute for Policy Innovation.   They note that Carr has roundly condemned ABC over its content, and in seeming direct echoes of Trump's condemnations — at one point saying on a right-wing podcast in September 2025 that ABC getting rid of Kimmel "can do this the easy way or the hard way." ABC suspended Kimmel hours later over remarks he made about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.   The suspension was soon lifted after a public outcry.   Fellow satirists Seth Meyers of NBC's Late Night and John Oliver of HBO's Last Week Tonight paid tribute to their ABC counterpart during an episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live taped last week in Brooklyn.   
   "You come up all the time. [Fans] will normally say, how does it feel, being disliked by the current president? And we always say, as long as you're on the air, we're fine," Oliver told Kimmel. "We are fully behind you — the way we're fully behind a bulletproof vest."   The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press has filed a friend of the court brief on ABC's behalf, hiring a former U.S. solicitor general who has argued repeatedly before the U.S. Supreme Court, to represent the organization at the district court level.   
   Bruce Brown, president of the group, pointed at a series of other actions by Carr and other Trump appointees: The FCC has launched investigations into all broadcast networks, including NPR (save Fox, which is controlled by the president's allies, Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch); The administration has cut off access for many journalists at the White House and the Pentagon, while federal agents sought access to journalists' devices to identify anonymous sources; all the while, the president has sought to delegitimize media outlets whose presentation of the news has sparked public displays of anger.   "This is only one part of a wide effort by the Trump administration to intimidate the press — and to try to coerce out of news organizations the type of coverage the president wants to see," Brown says.

schema.headline: Disney, ABC battle Trump's FCC in court over free speech protections
